title: Money Was Never One Thing

sourceEvidence.locator: PROLOGUE — THE MONEY IN YOUR POCKET IS STRANGER THAN YOU THINK
sourceEvidence.excerpt: You may have Swiss francs or euros in a bank account, a few banknotes, a credit-card limit, airline miles, loyalty points, gift cards, pension claims, a brokerage account, cryptoassets, perhaps a stablecoin balance, and credits inside one or more digital platforms. Some of these things can buy lunch. Some can buy an airline seat but not lunch. Some can be sold for money. Some can be transferred only under the rules of a company. Some expire. Some earn interest. Some exist only because a database says they do.

sourceEvidence.locator: PROLOGUE — THE MONEY IN YOUR POCKET IS STRANGER THAN YOU THINK
sourceEvidence.excerpt: We live, in other words, inside a multi-monetary economy while speaking as if money were singular.

sourceEvidence.locator: PROLOGUE — THE MONEY IN YOUR POCKET IS STRANGER THAN YOU THINK
sourceEvidence.excerpt: That linguistic habit matters because it hides the central question of this book. Money is not merely a neutral measuring stick that appeared once in history and then became more efficient. Monetary systems are designed institutions. They decide who can issue claims, who receives credit before possessing resources, whose promises circulate, what can be purchased, how losses are allocated, which debts are enforceable, and which forms of wealth can survive through time. To design money is to design part of society.

sourceEvidence.locator: PROLOGUE — THE MONEY IN YOUR POCKET IS STRANGER THAN YOU THINK
sourceEvidence.excerpt: The modern nation-state made a remarkable achievement out of suppressing this complexity. It created a world in which a vast territory could price most things in one unit, settle debts through one hierarchy of banks, collect taxes in one currency, and rely on a central bank to anchor the system. That simplification was enormously useful. It made prices comparable, contracts easier, markets larger, and monetary policy possible at national scale.

hook: Your wallet holds money that can buy lunch, money that expires, and promises you cannot freely transfer.
readerPromise: Recognize monetary systems as varied institutions that distribute claims, trust and social opportunity.
protectedRevelations: Specific monetary designs, case outcomes and final recommendations.
visualPlan: Keep several distinct forms of value in the wallet, showing their different usable contexts.
Place one balance beside its rules rather than presenting a currency as neutral substance.
Use selected historical forms at equal scale, avoiding a simple evolutionary ladder.
Return the differing promises to the wallet and hold the question of who stands behind them.
